item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Attack on Riyadh airport leaves 12 dead, more than 300 injured
item.description:
Attack on Riyadh airport leaves 12 dead, more than 300 injured

Submitted by MEE staff on Sun, 10/11/2026 - 01:03
Saudi-led military coalition vows 'firm' response as Trump says US may join strikes on Houthis
A Flynas plane lands at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 19 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

At least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh as Yemen's Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.  

The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Sunday that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack late on Saturday.

The authority said some of the injured were in critical condition and that all were receiving medical care at several hospitals.  

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter told Reuters. 

Jordan's foreign ministry said in a statement on Saturday that two injured Jordanians were discharged from hospital while two others were still receiving treatment. 

One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside.

More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility.

A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. 

Turkey to deploy troops and air defence systems to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
Read More »

This week's two previous attacks on the airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The Iran-aligned group, which is yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack, has warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there - except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina - is a target.

The attack on the airport comes amid escalating fighting between Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces and Houthis.  

Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, a spokesman for the government forces, said more than 1,900 operations carried out in the past 24 hours targeted weapons and ammunition depots, camps and military positions, reinforcements and other “military objectives deep within areas controlled” by the Houthis.

The coalition called the attack a "war crime" and said it will respond firmly to the attack on the airport, Reuters reported.

Advisories issued 

Flight-tracking site Flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted several carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences, including the World Petroleum Conference.

Organisers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, according to Reuters.

Saudi war against Houthis displaces 130,000 Yemenis as hunger crisis deepens
Read More »

In an advisory issued earlier on Saturday, King Khalid Airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic, without specifying the cause of the disruptions.

Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also instructed Saudi citizens travelling to the kingdom to contact local embassies if their travel itineraries have been disrupted following the attack.

At the same time, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in Saudi Arabia. 

The US embassy in Saudi Arabia urged Americans to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.

In a statement released on Sunday, the US Mission said US government employees working in the kingdom required special authorisation to use the King Khalid Airport, as well as airports in Jeddah and Dammam.

It said US government employees are not to travel within 20 miles (32km) of the Yemeni border due to safety risks, and need special authorisation for travel to the provinces of Jazan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif.

The UK and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”.

US may join

Following reports of the latest attack, United States President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether Washington planned to join the Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

“We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the ⁠⁠⁠⁠recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said.

“I think it’s terrible. The Saudis are good fighters but I think the attack was a terrible thing,” the US president said.

Saudi Arabia turns to UAE 'white horse' as it gears up to battle Yemen's Houthis
Read More »

Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman about it. He said the US had communication with the Houthis and added that “what they did was very bad”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia. He said an American citizen was killed in the strikes.

"These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X.

The attack was widely condemned, with Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs calling it “a direct threat to the security of the region”.

Qatar’s former prime minister said that today’s attack on King Khalid Airport shows that it is “more urgent than ever” to stand with Saudi Arabia in a “practical and decisive” manner. 

“It has now become clear that Iran is our primary adversary,” Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani said in a post on X, adding that the Gulf Cooperation Council today confronts “several hostile plots and conspiracies” that require “unity and profound foresight”.

He said it has become “more urgent and evident” that Qatar stands with Saudi Arabia against the “threat from within Yemen” that is being “plotted and directed from outside [Yemen]”.

The situation “necessitates setting aside all peripheral disputes” among Gulf Cooperation Council members and “demonstrating unity” instead, he said.

International reaction 

Japan’s embassy also “strongly” condemned Houthi attacks on airports and other Saudi civilian facilities.

Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights because the airport had closed due to a “security situation”.

Egypt's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed its “profound denunciation of these blatant attacks”, their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail.

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.

The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

item.description:
Centcom says cargo vessel trying to run Iran blockade disabled

The US military said it had disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored warnings and attempted to run an ongoing naval blockade against Iran.

"A U.S. military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew," the US Central Command (Centcom) posted on X.

Centcom said the cargo vessel had attempted to transit regional waters after leaving an Iranian port.

U.S. Forces Disable Cargo Vessel Attempting to Violate Blockade TAMPA, Fla. — U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Oct. 10, after the ship’s crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran. A U.S. military fighter jet struck the stern of Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica (also known as the “Arika Sun”) with a precision munition, fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew. The large cargo vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after having previously departed an Iranian port. CENTCOM forces resumed America’s blockade against all ships entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14. Four commercial vessels have been disabled and 135 ships have been turned around during three months of strict enforcement. Additionally, U.S. forces have destroyed 10 tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' multibillion-dollar shadow network over the same period. All mariners are advised to heed blockade warnings from CENTCOM forces. Crews should also continue to monitor Notice to Mariners broadcasts and contact U.S. naval forces on bridge-to-bridge channel 16 when operating in the Gulf of Oman and Strait of Hormuz approaches.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Hind Rajab Foundation seeks probe into Sde Teiman detainee abuse
item.description:
Hind Rajab Foundation seeks probe into Sde Teiman detainee abuse

The Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF) has asked the International Criminal Court prosecutor to investigate Israeli health and defence officials, the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) and medical staff over the alleged death, torture and ill-treatment of Palestinian detainees at the Sde Teiman detention facility since 7 October 2023.

In its Article 15 communication, HRF said the conduct of the accused amounts to war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide under the Rome Statute. Former health ministers Moshe Arbel and Uriel Buso and IMA president Zion Hagay have been named in the complaint.

It timed the filing to coincide with the World Medical Association (WMA) General Assembly in Rotterdam, which ran from 7 to 10 October.

HRF alleges a 19 December 2023 Health Ministry directive required staff to treat detainees handcuffed and blindfolded, barred them from identifying themselves by name, and authorised forced treatment without safeguards. It says at least 29 detainees had died at the site by November 2025.

The group also accuses the IMA of providing “institutional cover”, citing an April 2024 letter by IMA leaders in The American Journal of Bioethics saying detainees were receiving “appropriate medical care”. HRF said the IMA opened no disciplinary proceedings.

HRF Director General Dyab Abou Jahjah said the WMA "must answer why an association that provided institutional cover for torture is still welcome at its table".

🚨The #HindRajabFoundation has filed an Article 15 communication with the ICC calling for an investigation into Israeli officials, medical professionals and the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) over the death, torture and ill-treatment of Palestinian detainees at Sde Teiman. The submission argues that the conduct documented in the filing amounts to war crimes, crimes against humanity, and acts of genocide under the Rome Statute. ➡️ More → https://t.co/qhgnpNEhuX

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?
item.description:
Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight

It took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through which Christa Pike would be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.

“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Former Biden adviser says Netanyahu made 2024 Gaza deal ‘impossible’
item.description:
Former Biden adviser says Netanyahu made 2024 Gaza deal ‘impossible’

Phil Gordon, national security adviser to former US vice president Kamala Harris, has seconded allegations that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delayed a hostage-ceasefire deal in 2024.

Writing on X on Saturday, Gordon said Netanyahu added “so many of his own conditions” that the deal became “impossible for another six months”. He said nearly 9,000 more Palestinians were killed in that period, and more Israeli hostages died, including six executed by Hamas in August.

Gordon said the added Israeli demands included keeping forces along Gaza’s entire border with Egypt and a new mechanism to screen Gazans returning north. Both were dropped in the deal finally concluded in January 2025.

His comments follow a Channel 12 interview with Avi Gil, Netanyahu’s military secretary until May 2024, who alleged that Netanyahu passed up chances to bring hostages home alive because of the risk to his political career. Asked whether some could have been saved, he replied: “We could have.”

Gil also claimed Netanyahu was repeatedly warned before 7 October 2023, and that staff tampered with his phone records.

Netanyahu supporters seem to be taking advantage of @Brett_McGurk’s book and interviews to claim vindication for Netanyahu’s conduct of the war in Gaza. But while Brett’s front-row account is valuable, that doesn’t mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared—including among former members of the Biden administration. I would say most of my former colleagues think that President Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner, and few think that the biggest mistake Biden made was to show daylight with Israel. And even Brett’s account makes clear that hostages were not the top priority for Netanyahu and that when U.S. pressure actually was applied—as after the World Central Kitchen strike—it worked. Brett tells the story of the Biden phone call after that tragedy, but not the story of how Biden called Netanyahu on July 4, 2024 to press him to conclude the hostage deal after Hamas had finally accepted the basic framework, dropping its demand that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released. Netanyahu instead added so many of his own conditions—against the advice of his own security chiefs—that the deal became impossible for another six months, during which nearly 9,000 more Palestinians were killed and more Israeli hostages died, including the six that Hamas executed in August. The Israeli changes included a demand that Israel retain forces along Gaza’s entire border with Egypt, which the IDF had seized only after the original proposal, and a new enforcement mechanism to screen Gazans who were returning home to the north which would have required Israeli troops to remain in central Gaza. Both of those new conditions were dropped in the deal ultimately concluded in January 2025. Nothing in the book or elsewhere changes the reality that October 7 happened on Netanyahu’s watch; that he prioritized “total victory” and the maintenance of his coalition over a hostage deal or an end of the war; that his conduct of the war and management of its humanitarian consequences catastrophic; that it has left Israel more isolated and insecure; and that it has deeply damaged, perhaps irreparably, Israel’s relationship with the United States—which should have done more to change Israel’s conduct rather than enable it. There was never an easy way forward in Gaza, but no version of the story vindicates Netanyahu.

— Phil Gordon (@PhilGordonDC) October 10, 2026
